Mutual Funds Explained: Types, NAV, Structure, SIP and Costs

A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in a professionally managed portfolio. This guide covers its structure, how NAV is worked out, the fund types, and what it costs.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

How a mutual fund is structured

An Indian mutual fund is set up as a trust, in a three-tier structure designed to separate the money from the people managing it.

TierRole
SponsorSets up the mutual fund, like a promoter
TrusteesProtect unit holders' interests and oversee the AMC
Asset management company (AMC)Manages the investments
Custodian and registrar (RTA)Keep the securities safe and maintain investor records

All of them operate under SEBI's mutual fund regulations.

NAV: the price of a unit

NAV = (market value of assets − liabilities) ÷ number of units. A scheme with assets of ₹100 crore, liabilities of ₹1 crore and 5 crore units has an NAV of ₹99 crore ÷ 5 crore = ₹19.80.

A low NAV does not make a fund cheap. A ₹20 NAV and a ₹200 NAV fund with identical portfolios give the same percentage return.

Types of mutual funds

TypeInvests inTypically suits
Equity funds (large, mid, small cap, flexi cap, sector)Mainly sharesGoals 5 to 7 years or more away
ELSSShares, with a 3-year lock-inTax saving under the old regime
Debt funds (liquid, short duration, gilt, corporate bond)Bonds and money market instrumentsShorter goals and stability
Hybrid fundsA mix of equity and debtA balance of growth and stability
Index funds and ETFsA copy of an index such as NIFTY 50Low-cost, passive investing
Fund of fundsOther fundsInternational and multi-asset exposure

Open-ended and closed-ended

Open-ended funds accept and redeem money every business day at NAV. Closed-ended funds have a fixed term and raise money only at launch; they list on an exchange so that investors can exit, often below NAV.

Ways of investing: SIP, lump sum, STP and SWP

  • SIP: a fixed amount each month, which brings rupee cost averaging.
  • Lump sum: a one-time investment.
  • STP: regular transfers from one fund to another.
  • SWP: regular withdrawals from a fund, often used in retirement.

What you pay

  • Expense ratio: a yearly fee taken from the fund's assets. It lowers the NAV daily, so you never see a separate bill.
  • Exit load: a fee on early redemption in some funds.
  • Direct and regular plans: a direct plan has no distributor commission, so its returns are higher over time than the same fund's regular plan.
  • Tax: gains are taxed depending on the type of fund and how long you hold it. Check the current rules.

Active and passive

An active fund's manager tries to beat a benchmark, for a higher fee. A passive fund simply copies the index, for a lower fee. To judge an active fund, compare its returns with its benchmark after costs, over periods of several years, and look at risk measures such as alpha and the Sharpe ratio.

Exam and interview questions

How is NAV calculated?

NAV = (market value of assets − liabilities) ÷ number of units outstanding. It is published at the end of each business day.

Who are the parties in a mutual fund?

The sponsor, the trustees, the asset management company, the custodian and the registrar and transfer agent, all regulated by SEBI.

Does a lower NAV mean a better fund?

No. Returns depend on how the portfolio's value changes in percentage terms, not on the level of NAV.
